results.title: Best Practices for Documenting Risks, Assumptions, and Constraints in System Architecture
results.content: # What are the best practices for documenting risks, assumptions, and constraints in system architecture? Why document risks, assumptions, and constraints? How to document risks, assumptions, and constraints? What are the best practices for documenting risks, assumptions, and constraints? What are the challenges and pitfalls of documenting risks, assumptions, and constraints? Therefore, it is also important to document the risks, assumptions, and constraints that affect the system architecture and its implementation. In this article, we will discuss the best practices for documenting risks, assumptions, and constraints in system architecture. Documenting risks, assumptions, and constraints helps to identify and mitigate the uncertainties and challenges that could affect the system architecture and its success. ## 2 Why document risks, assumptions, and constraints? Documenting risks, assumptions, and constraints has several benefits for system architecture. ## 3 How to document risks, assumptions, and constraints? Documenting risks, assumptions, and constraints is not a one-time activity, but rather an ongoing, collaborative process. ## 4 What are the best practices for documenting risks, assumptions, and constraints? Documenting risks, assumptions, and constraints is a critical and complex process, so it’s essential to follow some best practices to ensure its effectiveness and efficiency. Involve relevant stakeholders and experts in the identification and analysis of the risks, assumptions, and constraints. Document the risks, assumptions, and constraints as early and detailed as possible in the system architecture lifecycle. ## 5 What are the challenges and pitfalls of documenting risks, assumptions, and constraints? Documenting risks, assumptions, and constraints is not a flawless or perfect process, but rather a prone and imperfect one. These may include overlooking or underestimating risks, assumptions, or constraints that could have a major impact on the system architecture or its outcomes. Furthermore, failing to document or communicate the risks, assumptions, or constraints clearly and promptly with the stakeholders or developers could be detrimental. Moreover, conflicting or inconsistent risks, assumptions, or constraints among the stakeholders and developers as well as having too many or too few of them can cause problems with the system architecture process or quality. results.title: Project Orbis — harmonizing up or down?
results.content: Is speed the only thing that’s important when approving new cancer drugs? Founded in 2019, “Project Orbis” supports collaborative and simultaneous review of cancer drugs across eight countries to harmonize decisions. Given that drugs are almost always launched first in the US, the underpinning idea is that simultaneous regulatory review can speed up approval and access to promising cancer treatments in other countries. This year the Swiss regulator found that Project Orbis speeds time to regulatory approval00158-X/fulltext). Also, health technology assessments are required in many partner countries given public systems to reimburse these drugs. In our new work published in The Lancet Oncology, we asked whether the drugs reviewed through this program are better than the ones approved through other FDA pathways. We followed these drugs from FDA approval to health technology assessment bodies in the UK and Canada — the organisations responsible for reimbursement under public insurance plans, and estimated their list prices. **The clinical gains of drugs reviewed through Project Orbis are no different than those reviewed through other FDA programs.**. The clinical benefits (defined as gains in overall or progression-free survival) of drugs reviewed through Project Orbis were not statistically different than among all FDA approvals over the same period. It’s important to note that many of the drugs reviewed through Project Orbis are immunotherapies and may be high benefit for a subset of patients. The FDA states that the criteria for drugs reviewed through Project Orbis are that cancer drugs must be clinically significant and ideally meet the criteria for the priority review pathway. However, there is limited transparency beyond this statement, raising questions about how the FDA selects drugs to be reviewed through this program and what clinical benefits patients receive. While the program has facilitated faster regulatory review times, health technology assessment decisions take a median of 350 days. This raises the question of whether Project Orbis speeds access in partner countries, as access is typically limited until after a favourable review. Speeding up access to promising drugs is only advantageous when patients (and health systems) can afford them. **Project Orbis — the start of many other initiatives to globalize FDA standards?**.
